sections.title: Geographic Imbalance in Publishing
sections.text: The academic publishing ecosystem remains significantly unbalanced, with the majority of international journals possessing wide reach situated in Western countries [1]. This concentration results in limited distribution of scholarly content to nations in the Global South and other regions [1]. Consequently, the global flow of academic knowledge is skewed toward Western-centric outlets, leaving researchers in developing countries with fewer direct avenues for international dissemination [1].

To address this gap, the CARPET platform provides essential information on e-publishing technology and supports the sustainability of existing e-publishing projects and their solutions [3]. sections.title: Disintermediation of Publisher Control
sections.text: The rise of open access, academic social networks, and piracy websites has diminished the total control publishers previously held over how academics access published content [5]. Open access publications can now proliferate across the web through the use of Creative Commons licenses, allowing for permission-free sharing of content without requiring mediation by publisher portals [5]. These articles appear in a diverse range of locations, including faculty websites, institutional and subject repositories, and academic social networks, all of which legally circumvent traditional publisher portals [5]. This fragmentation of distribution channels challenges the traditional gatekeeping role of commercial publishers.

sections.title: Foundational Model Capabilities
sections.text: Large language models function as artificial intelligence systems whose primary knowledge consists of statistical patterns, semantic relationships, and syntactical structures of language [1]. Despite these limited forms of knowledge, these systems are adept at numerous complex tasks, including creative writing, storytelling, and translation [1]. This foundational capability provides the basis for integrating external structural data to enhance scientific processing.

sections.title: Structural Properties of Citation Graphs
sections.text: The citation graph offers unique structural information regarding document-level relatedness that extends beyond intra-document information [3]. In this graph, adjacent paper nodes share related scientific terms and topics [3]. Furthermore, reference papers within a research community are very similar in content, logic, and writing style to the source paper, as exemplified by papers focused on the Weak Galerkin Finite Element Method [2]. These shared characteristics make the graph a valuable resource for capturing context that text alone may miss.

This integration provides an increase in end-to-end information extraction system performance over strong baselines [4].

question: How have theories of distributed cognition informed the design of features in social computing systems?

sections.title: Theoretical Foundations
sections.text: Distributed cognition has been proposed as a new foundation for human-computer interaction, offering a radical reorientation of design principles [4][4]. As a theory, it is specifically tailored to understanding interactions among people and technologies, providing an effective framework for designing and evaluating digital systems [4][3]. The theory identifies cognitive agents, processes, and events that exist within an environment and beyond the 'skin or skull of an individual' [3]. This perspective shifts focus from individual skills to environmental factors, as demonstrated in an aircraft cockpit case study [3]. Furthermore, the theory is compatible with different users encountering different features of the same experience [2]. A model has been developed to visualize different theoretical aspects of the theory of distributed cognition [1].

sections.title: Integration with Social Psychology
sections.text: Theories of social psychology and cognitive science provide diverse and enlightening perspectives on group dynamics, adaptive behavior, and networks of social relationships [1]. Research has explicitly framed group intelligence through the lens of distributed cognition [1]. This integration allows for a deeper understanding of how cognitive processes are distributed across social groups and technological artifacts.

sections.title: Design Patterns and Experiments
sections.text: Researchers have examined different design patterns for distributed cognition in a controlled experiment among software practitioners [5]. These experiments help identify how specific design choices influence cognitive distribution and collaboration. The findings from such studies inform the development of systems that support distributed cognitive processes effectively.

sections.title: Application to Social Media Feeds
sections.text: Recent work addresses the design of usable controls for customizable social media feeds, directly tackling social computing feature design [6]. This research applies the Interactive Machine Teaching (IMT) framework to feed customization [6]. A key challenge identified in this context is the natural tradeoff between the expressiveness of a system and its understandability [6]. Balancing these factors is crucial for creating effective social computing tools that support distributed cognition.

question: How has literature discussed AI as a design material?

sections.title: Conceptualization of AI as Material
sections.text: The Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) community has recently highlighted artificial intelligence as a design material [2]. This conceptual shift serves as a call for interaction designers to treat intelligence as a fundamental resource for design [2]. By viewing intelligence as a material, the field recognizes a need to better understand how it functions within design processes [2]. Researchers and designers have investigated this idea to explore AI's potential in improving interactions with applications and software systems [1].

sections.title: Practitioner Challenges and Skill Gaps
sections.text: Working with AI as a design material presents significant challenges, including the inherent complexity of the material itself [4]. HCI and design researchers have extensively discussed these difficulties, noting a lack of clear understanding of AI's capabilities and the struggle to envision uses that do not yet exist [3]. Designers, who are often machine learning novices, experience specific difficulties and bottlenecks while working with AI [1]. These obstacles highlight the gap between current design practices and the technical demands of integrating intelligent systems.

question: How is artificial intelligence being utilized to enhance the diagnosis and treatment of sleep apnea?

sections.title: Clinical Context and Diagnostic Challenges
sections.text: Sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (SAHS) is a chronic, highly prevalent disease considered a major health problem in industrialized countries [3]. Despite advocacy for new diagnostic methods in the last decade, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) remains underdiagnosed and untreated in a significant number of adult patients [4]. The gold standard for diagnosis is in-laboratory nocturnal polysomnography (PSG) [3]. This process involves identifying sleep stages in an overnight polysomnogram, which utilizes EEG as one sensing modality [2]. However, the traditional visual scoring of these stages suffers from subjectivity and inter-rater variability [2]. To address these limitations, machine learning could represent a relevant step forward in the intricate scenario of sleep apnea diagnosis and phenotypization [1].

snippets: In this perspective, machine learning could represent a relevant step forward in the intricate scenario of sleep apnea diagnosis and phenotypization.

So far, the most important applications of artificial intelligence in obstructive sleep apnea have been the following: (1) predicting treatment outcomes of various treatment options, (2) improving treatment options, and (3) personalizing treatment thanks to the enhanced understanding of underlying mechanisms of the disease [58].

sections.title: AI-Driven Diagnostic Techniques
sections.text: Machine-learning technologies have been widely implemented for the analysis of big data and the development of prediction tools [4]. Specific applications include the use of Recurrent Deep Neural Networks for real-time sleep stage classification from single-channel EEG, as demonstrated by Bresch et al. in 2018 [2]. Additionally, a state space and density estimation framework has been developed for sleep staging in obstructive sleep apnea, as described by Kang et al. in 2018 [2]. Further advancements involve the automated identification of sleep disorder types using a triplet half-band filter and ensemble ML with EEG signals, a method proposed by Sharma et al. in 2021 [5]. These computational approaches aim to reduce the subjectivity inherent in manual scoring and improve the accuracy of diagnostic phenotyping [1].

sections.title: Screening via Cardiac Monitoring
sections.text: Beyond direct polysomnography, AI is being utilized in cardiac contexts to screen for sleep apnea. A pilot study demonstrated the significance of using 24-hour ECG analysis to determine the sleep apnea index (AI) in patients with heart rhythm disorders [6]. This approach helps establish the cause of rhythm issues and determines further diagnosis and treatment [6]. Clinical protocols indicate that patients with an AI greater than 5 are referred for further diagnostic evaluation of sleep apnea [6]. This integration of cardiac data with sleep metrics provides an additional pathway for identifying at-risk individuals who might otherwise remain undiagnosed [4].

sections.title: Treatment Optimization and Personalization
sections.text: The most important applications of artificial intelligence in obstructive sleep apnea currently involve predicting treatment outcomes of various options, improving treatment options, and personalizing treatment [1]. If sleep apnea is confirmed in a specialized laboratory, the application of CPAP is considered the best form of treatment [6]. AI tools support this by helping to predict which patients will respond well to such interventions [1]. In addition to device-based therapy, patients are advised to correct living habits, reduce or eliminate the use of medications that predispose them to respiratory distress such as sedatives, and visit throat specialists to correct existing anatomical anomalies [6]. By combining predictive modeling with these clinical guidelines, AI enhances the precision of therapeutic strategies [1].
